comments.author: @BrockMcLellan
comments.text:
No, Cascadia is not a country. It is a state of mind. I grew up in British Columbia (BC), living there from 1948 to 1980. After that I moved to Norway, where I continue to live. Many people in BC felt that the main eastern border was the Rocky Mountains. Beyond that, in Alberta and beyond were the Easterners, who never really understood our mountainous homeland. I think that boundary also applied within British Columbia itself, excluding the Peace River district. Yes, easterners could keep that territory as well. There was also an affinity with those American to the north (living in the Alaska panhandle) and to the south, mainly Washington state. For me the Columbia River between Washington and Oregon was one limit, but many wanted Cascadia to include Oregon, possibly even Idaho. Indeed, on a good day, some might be willing to include Big Sky, Bozeman and Butte in Montana, although Billings was a step too far. Fewer places in Wyoming met with Cascadian approval. On a good day, Yellowstone, but not Buffalo, or Casper. 

For those of us with such an identity, we had little understanding about the mindset of easterners, starting with the farmers in the near east of the prairie provinces, or those living beyond in the mid east of Ontario and Quebec or the far east of the Maritime provinces. We could not understand how an easterner living in Chicago could describe themselves as living in the mid-west. For us, it too was the middle east, with an incomprehensible culture.

comments.text: It’s worth knowing that narrow strips of mountain chains slid northward parallel to each other, defining the west coast of North America. These rafts of stone started roughly along the coast of Mexico about 70 million years ago, and to this day, proceed north at a speed of about an inch a year, sliding next each other. So, much of the Alaska archipelago, the mountain ranges of BC and the coast range of Oregon and Washington are parallel stripes of varied granite, causing some of the larger North American plate to rotate slowly north.

comments.author: @MistyRainne
comments.text:
Driving from the Willamette Valley to the coast goes through a lot of forests with roads cut through them. It's like driving through a canyon. Beautiful in its own way even before reaching the coast itself. (But the coast is the sort of place you wear a jacket to even in summer.)

I dunno why it's relatively non-religious. We're not the only place in the world with mountains and forests. If anything I would think it'd make people _more_ religious to see the world in all its glory. But like most places in the world, most of the population are city folk.

As for the volcanoes, we're part of the Pacific Ring Of Fire; so we have that connection too with Japan and other places along the Pacific. The Juan de Fuca Plate is a remnant of the once-vast Farallon Plate being subducted under the Americas (there are some other remnants down in Central/South America). It's probably where the Rocky Mountains came from, and California's geography largely comes from scraping off various stuff from former lands that have since been subducted.

In general, I like it here. It's a nice place that gets overlooked a lot, so all the flies that get drawn to popularity go elsewhere.
